# Overview



TranscriptFormer is a family of **generative foundation models** for single-cell transcriptomics that learns rich, context-aware representations of cells by jointly modeling genes and their expression levels. Trained on up to 112 million cells spanning 1.53 billion years of evolution across 12 species, it represents a **cross-species generative cell atlas** — a single model architecture that can encode, reconstruct, and compare transcriptomes from organisms as diverse as humans, fruit flies, and freshwater sponges. Whether you want to extract cell embeddings for clustering, compute contextual gene embeddings for downstream analysis, or predict expression counts autoregressively, TranscriptFormer provides a unified CLI and model interface to do so.

![Model Overview](https://github.com/czi-ai/transcriptformer/blob/main/assets/model_overview.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L52)

## What TranscriptFormer Does

At its core, TranscriptFormer treats each cell as a **sentence of genes** — a sequence of gene tokens, each paired with an expression count — and processes it through a transformer encoder to produce two kinds of outputs. **Cell embeddings** are mean-pooled vectors summarizing the entire transcriptomic state of a cell, useful for clustering, annotation, and cross-species comparison. **Contextual gene embeddings** capture how each gene is represented within the context of a specific cell, enabling gene-level analyses such as functional similarity and gene program discovery. During training, the model also learns to **autoregressively predict** gene identity and expression levels, making it a generative model capable of reconstructing transcriptomes.

The model's power comes from three design pillars working together: **pretrained protein embeddings** from ESM-2 provide biologically grounded gene representations without requiring the model to learn gene semantics from scratch; a **Flex Attention Transformer Encoder** with causal masking and count-based attention bias allows the model to attend over gene sequences while conditioning on expression magnitudes; and a **Zero-Truncated Poisson loss** properly handles the discrete, non-zero count data that characterizes single-cell RNA sequencing. These components are described in depth in the [Architecture Overview](4-architecture-overview) page.

Sources: [model.py](/src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L217-L317), [layers.py](/src/transcriptformer/model/layers.py#L44-L99), [losses.py](/src/transcriptformer/model/losses.py#L101-L163)

## Model Variants at a Glance

TranscriptFormer ships as three pretrained checkpoints, each designed for a different breadth of biological coverage. All three share the same architecture but differ in training data, vocabulary size, and parameter count. Choosing the right variant depends on your species of interest and the level of cross-species generalization you need.

| Variant | Training Data | Trainable Params | Frozen Params (ESM-2) | Vocabulary Size | Best For |
|---------|--------------|-------------------|------------------------|-----------------|----------|
| **TF-Sapiens** | 57M human cells | 368M | 61M | 23,829 | Human-only studies; smallest footprint |
| **TF-Exemplar** | 110M cells (human + 4 model organisms) | 542M | 282M | 110,290 | Cross-species work across common model organisms |
| **TF-Metazoa** | 112M cells (12 species spanning Metazoa + Fungi + Protista) | 444M | 633M | 247,388 | Broadest evolutionary coverage; invertebrate and non-model species |

> [!TIP]
> TF-Metazoa has fewer trainable parameters than TF-Exemplar despite covering more species because its ESM-2 embeddings (which are frozen) are larger. The total parameter count is actually higher — 1.08B vs 824M — but the trainable fraction is smaller.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L19-L44)

## Architecture at a High Level

The following diagram shows the end-to-end data flow through TranscriptFormer, from raw AnnData input through embedding extraction and count prediction. Each block maps to a dedicated module in the codebase.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["📄 AnnData Input<br/>(raw counts + gene IDs)"] --> B["🔤 Gene Tokenizer<br/>& Vocabulary Lookup"]
    B --> C["🧬 Pretrained Embeddings<br/>(ESM-2 protein embeddings → MLP projection)"]
    A --> D["🔢 Count Encoding<br/>(log1p of clipped counts)"]
    C --> E["⚡ Flex Attention<br/>Transformer Encoder"]
    D --> E
    E --> F{"Output Type?"}
    F -->|"Cell Embeddings"| G["📊 Mean-Pooling<br/>over gene positions"]
    F -->|"Contextual Gene<br/>Embeddings"| H["🔬 Per-Gene<br/>Transformer Output"]
    F -->|"Generative"| I["📈 Count Decoder Head<br/>(ZTP loss)"]
    F -->|"Gene ID<br/>Prediction"| J["🏷️ Gene ID Head<br/>(Cross-Entropy loss)"]
    
    style A fill:#e8f4e8,stroke:#2d7a2d
    style E fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#2563eb
    style G fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706
    style H fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706
    style I fill:#fce7f3,stroke:#db2777
    style J fill:#fce7f3,stroke:#db2777
```

Key architectural details to note: the transformer uses **causal masking** (each gene attends only to preceding genes) combined with a **count-based attention bias** (expression magnitude modulates attention scores), enforced through PyTorch's `flex_attention` with compiled block masks. The **Count Decoder Head** receives a concatenated skip-connection of transformer output and input gene embeddings (doubling the effective dimension), then applies a link function — by default `softmax` over the gene axis, scaled by total cell counts — to produce rate parameters for the Zero-Truncated Poisson distribution. This generative formulation is what distinguishes TranscriptFormer from purely embedding-based models.

Sources: [model.py](/src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L217-L317), [layers.py](/src/transcriptformer/model/layers.py#L271-L344), [masks.py](/src/transcriptformer/model/masks.py#L1-L17), [losses.py](/src/transcriptformer/model/losses.py#L101-L163)

## Cross-Species Design

A defining feature of TranscriptFormer is its ability to operate across species boundaries. During training, all species share the same transformer weights, but each gene is represented by its **ESM-2 protein embedding** — meaning that orthologous genes with similar protein sequences naturally receive similar representations, even if they have never been seen together during training. For species not included in any training set (out-of-distribution species like rat, pig, or chimpanzee), TranscriptFormer supports **embedding surgery**: swapping the gene embedding layer with one constructed from the new species' ESM-2 embeddings while preserving all other model weights. This allows zero-shot transfer to entirely new organisms without retraining.

The pretrained embedding files for 24 species (12 in-distribution + 12 out-of-distribution) are available for download via the CLI. If you need a species not covered by these pre-generated embeddings, you can produce your own ESM-2 protein embeddings and perform embedding surgery using the utilities in the `preprocess/` directory.

Sources: [embedding_surgery.py](/src/transcriptformer/model/embedding_surgery.py#L8-L80), [vocab.py](/src/transcriptformer/tokenizer/vocab.py#L10-L62), [README.md](/README.md#L88-L136)

## Project Structure

The codebase is organized around clean separation between model definition, data handling, tokenization, and CLI orchestration:

```
transcriptformer/
├── cli/                          # Command-line interface
│   ├── conf/                     # Hydra configuration files
│   │   └── inference_config.yaml # Default inference configuration
│   ├── download_artifacts.py     # Model checkpoint & embedding downloader
│   ├── download_data.py          # CellxGene dataset downloader
│   └── inference.py              # Inference pipeline orchestration
├── data/                         # Data loading & processing
│   ├── bulk_download.py          # Bulk dataset download from CellxGene
│   ├── dataclasses.py            # Config dataclasses (Model, Data, Loss, Inference)
│   └── dataloader.py             # PyTorch DataLoader construction
├── datasets.py                   # Dataset classes for training & inference
├── model/                        # Core model implementation
│   ├── model.py                  # Transcriptformer & ESM2CE modules
│   ├── layers.py                 # Transformer, attention, embeddings, decoder
│   ├── losses.py                 # ZTP NLL & Cross-Entropy losses
│   ├── masks.py                  # Causal & padding mask factories
│   ├── embedding_surgery.py      # Cross-species embedding swap
│   └── inference.py              # Lightning-based inference runner
├── tokenizer/                    # Gene tokenization & vocabulary
│   ├── tokenizer.py              # Gene expression tokenizer
│   └── vocab.py                  # Vocabulary construction & ESM-2 loading
└── utils/                        # Shared utilities
    └── utils.py                  # Helper functions (embedding loading, etc.)
```

> [!TIP]
> The `ESM2CE` class in `model.py` inherits from `Transcriptformer` and overrides the forward pass to return raw ESM-2 embeddings without transformer processing — it serves as a baseline comparison model referenced in the paper. You can select it via `--model-type esm2ce` at inference time.

Sources: [model.py](/src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L443-L527), [dataclasses.py](/src/transcriptformer/data/dataclasses.py#L1-L200), [inference_config.yaml](/conf/inference_config.yaml#L1-L36)

## Quick Start Preview

Getting started with TranscriptFormer follows a three-step workflow: **install** the package, **download** a model checkpoint, and **run inference** on your data. The CLI handles all of this:

```bash
# 1. Install
uv pip install transcriptformer

# 2. Download a model
transcriptformer download tf-sapiens

# 3. Run inference
transcriptformer inference \
  --checkpoint-path ./checkpoints/tf_sapiens \
  --data-file your_data.h5ad \
  --output-path ./results \
  --batch-size 8
```

Input data must be in **H5AD (AnnData) format** with Ensembl gene IDs in the `var` dataframe and raw (unnormalized) count data in `X` or `raw.X`. The model handles all preprocessing internally — count clipping, vocabulary filtering, and log-transformation — so no manual normalization is required. Output is also an H5AD file, with cell embeddings stored in `obsm['embeddings']` by default.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L54-L80), [README.md](/README.md#L157-L210), [inference_config.yaml](/conf/inference_config.yaml#L1-L36)

# Quick Start



Get TranscriptFormer up and running in minutes — from installation to your first cell embeddings. This page walks you through the three essential stages: **install the package**, **download a model**, and **run inference** on your single-cell data. By the end, you will have produced an AnnData file containing context-aware embeddings ready for downstream analysis.

![TranscriptFormer Overview](https://github.com/czi-ai/transcriptformer/blob/main/assets/model_overview.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L8), [README.md](/README.md#L15-L32)

---

## Prerequisites

Before you begin, ensure your environment meets these requirements:

| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Python** | ≥ 3.11 (3.11 or 3.12 supported) |
| **Package manager** | [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) (recommended) or pip |
| **GPU** | NVIDIA GPU recommended (A100 40GB ideal); 16 GB VRAM works with batch size 1–4 |
| **PyTorch** | ≤ 2.5.1 (2.6.0+ may cause pickle errors) |

> [!TIP]
> On systems with limited VRAM, set `--batch-size 1` or `--batch-size 4` to avoid out-of-memory errors. You can also use the `--oom-dataloader` flag for datasets that don't fit in memory.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L35-L86), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L12-L34)

---

## Installation

TranscriptFormer can be installed from PyPI or from source. The `transcriptformer` CLI becomes available after installation.

### Install from PyPI (Recommended)

```bash
# Create and activate a virtual environment
uv venv --python=3.11
source .venv/bin/activate  # On Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate

# Install from PyPI
uv pip install transcriptformer
```

### Install from Source

Choose this path if you plan to contribute or need the latest unreleased changes.

```bash
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/czi-ai/transcriptformer.git
cd transcriptformer

# Create and activate a virtual environment
uv venv --python=3.11
source .venv/bin/activate  # On Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate

# Install in development (editable) mode
uv pip install -e .
```

### Verify Installation

```bash
transcriptformer --help
```

You should see three subcommands: `inference`, `download`, and `download-data`.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L35-L63), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L6-L55)

---

## Workflow Overview

The quickest path from zero to embeddings follows three sequential steps:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["📦 Install\ntranscriptformer"] --> B["⬇️ Download\nModel Weights"]
    B --> C["🧬 Run\nInference"]
    C --> D["📊 Embeddings\nin .h5ad"]

    style A fill:#6b3fa0,color:#fff
    style B fill:#7e4fbf,color:#fff
    style C fill:#9168d9,color:#fff
    style D fill:#a98ef0,color:#fff
```

Each step maps to a single CLI command — no Python scripting required for the standard workflow.

---

## Step 1 — Download Model Weights

TranscriptFormer ships three model variants, each pretrained on a different scope of species. Choose the one that matches your analysis needs:

| Model | Species Scope | Trainable Params | Vocab Size | Use When |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **TF-Sapiens** | Human only | 368 M | 23,829 | You only need human cell embeddings |
| **TF-Exemplar** | Human + 4 model organisms | 542 M | 110,290 | You need cross-species analysis across common model organisms |
| **TF-Metazoa** | 12 species (broadest) | 444 M | 247,388 | You need the widest evolutionary coverage including invertebrates |

Run the download command for your chosen model:

```bash
# Download a specific model
transcriptformer download tf-sapiens
# Or: transcriptformer download tf-exemplar
# Or: transcriptformer download tf-metazoa

# Download all models and extra species embeddings at once
transcriptformer download all

# Download only the extra protein embeddings (for out-of-distribution species)
transcriptformer download all-embeddings

# Specify a custom checkpoint directory (default: ./checkpoints)
transcriptformer download tf-sapiens --checkpoint-dir /path/to/custom/dir
```

After download, the checkpoint directory has this structure:

```
checkpoints/
├── tf_sapiens/
│   ├── model_weights.pt      # Trained model weights
│   ├── config.json           # Model architecture config
│   └── vocabs/               # Gene vocabulary files
├── tf_exemplar/
├── tf_metazoa/
└── all_embeddings/           # Protein embeddings for 24 species
    ├── mus_musculus_gene.h5
    ├── rattus_norvegicus_gene.h5
    └── ...
```

> [!TIP]
> Models come bundled with protein embeddings for their training species. If you need to run inference on a species *not* in the training set (e.g., rat with TF-Sapiens), also download `all-embeddings` or provide a custom embedding file via `--pretrained-embedding`.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L92-L151), [src/transcriptformer/cli/download_artifacts.py](/src/transcriptformer/cli/download_artifacts.py#L64-L122)

---

## Step 2 — Prepare Your Input Data

TranscriptFormer accepts **H5AD files** (the standard AnnData format) with minimal preparation:

| Requirement | Details |
|---|---|
| **Gene identifiers** | `adata.var` must contain an `ensembl_id` column with Ensembl gene IDs (e.g., `ENSG00000000003`). Changeable via `--gene-col-name`. |
| **Expression data** | **Raw (unnormalized) count data** — the model handles all transformations internally. It reads `adata.raw.X` first, then falls back to `adata.X`. |
| **Count clipping** | Counts are clipped at 30 by default (matching training). Adjustable via `--clip-counts`. |
| **Vocabulary filtering** | Out-of-vocabulary genes are automatically filtered. Only genes in the model's vocabulary are used. |

**No additional normalization, log-transformation, or scaling is needed.** The model processes raw counts as-is.

For experimenting, the repository ships small validation datasets you can use immediately:

```
test/data/
├── human_val.h5ad
├── mouse_val.h5ad
└── chicken_val.h5ad
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L303-L341)

---

## Step 3 — Run Inference

With a model downloaded and an H5AD file ready, run inference with a single command:

### Basic Inference (In-Distribution Species)

```bash
transcriptformer inference \
  --checkpoint-path ./checkpoints/tf_sapiens \
  --data-file test/data/human_val.h5ad \
  --output-path ./inference_results \
  --batch-size 8
```

### Out-of-Distribution Species

To run a model on a species it was *not* trained on, supply the protein embedding file:

```bash
transcriptformer inference \
  --checkpoint-path ./checkpoints/tf_sapiens \
  --data-file test/data/mouse_val.h5ad \
  --pretrained-embedding ./checkpoints/all_embeddings/mus_musculus_gene.h5 \
  --batch-size 8
```

### Extract Contextual Gene Embeddings

By default the CLI produces **cell embeddings** (mean-pooled across all genes). To get per-gene contextual embeddings instead, switch the embedding type:

```bash
transcriptformer inference \
  --checkpoint-path ./checkpoints/tf_sapiens \
  --data-file test/data/human_val.h5ad \
  --emb-type cge \
  --batch-size 8
```

### Key CLI Options at a Glance

| Flag | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `--checkpoint-path` | *(required)* | Path to the model checkpoint directory |
| `--data-file` | *(required)* | Path to input H5AD file |
| `--output-path` | `./inference_results` | Directory for saving results |
| `--output-filename` | `embeddings.h5ad` | Name of the output file |
| `--batch-size` | `8` | Samples per batch (reduce for low VRAM) |
| `--emb-type` | `cell` | `cell` = mean-pooled embeddings; `cge` = contextual gene embeddings |
| `--pretrained-embedding` | `None` | Path to protein embeddings for OOD species |
| `--precision` | `16-mixed` | Numerical precision (`16-mixed` or `32`) |
| `--num-gpus` | `1` | Number of GPUs (`-1` for all available) |
| `--device` | `auto` | Device: `auto`, `cpu`, `cuda`, or `mps` |
| `--oom-dataloader` | `False` | Enable OOM-safe data loading for large datasets |
| `--config-override` | — | Override any config value (e.g., `model.data_config.normalize_to_scale=10000`) |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L215-L301), [src/transcriptformer/cli/__init__.py](/src/transcriptformer/cli/__init__.py#L93-L221)

---

## Understanding Your Output

Inference produces an AnnData file (default: `./inference_results/embeddings.h5ad`) with the following structure:

**Cell embeddings** (`--emb-type cell`, default):

| Key | Location | Shape | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `obsm['embeddings']` | AnnData object | `(n_cells, embedding_dim)` | Mean-pooled cell representations |
| `obs` | AnnData object | — | Original cell metadata preserved |
| `uns['llh']` | AnnData object | — | Log-likelihood scores (if available) |

**Contextual gene embeddings** (`--emb-type cge`):

| Key | Location | Shape | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `uns['cge_embeddings']` | AnnData object | `(n_gene_instances, embedding_dim)` | Per-gene contextual representations |
| `uns['cge_cell_indices']` | AnnData object | `(n_gene_instances,)` | Cell index each gene embedding belongs to |
| `uns['cge_gene_names']` | AnnData object | `(n_gene_instances,)` | Gene name for each embedding |

### Quick Post-Inference Access

```python
import anndata as ad

# Load cell embeddings
adata = ad.read_h5ad("./inference_results/embeddings.h5ad")
cell_embeddings = adata.obsm['embeddings']  # (n_cells, embedding_dim)

# Load contextual gene embeddings
cge = ad.read_h5ad("./inference_results/cge_embeddings.h5ad")
gene_embs = cge.uns['cge_embeddings']       # (n_gene_instances, embedding_dim)
cell_idx = cge.uns['cge_cell_indices']       # which cell each gene belongs to
gene_names = cge.uns['cge_gene_names']       # gene identifier strings
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L343-L397)

---

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

| Problem | Cause | Solution |
|---|---|---|
| `pickle` / `Unpickling` error | PyTorch ≥ 2.6.0 | Downgrade: `uv pip install torch==2.5.1` |
| CUDA out-of-memory | Batch size too large for GPU | Reduce `--batch-size` to 1–4 |
| Dataset too large for RAM | Full H5AD loaded into memory | Add `--oom-dataloader --n-data-workers 4` |
| Low gene overlap warning | Many genes filtered from vocabulary | Check that `adata.var` contains correct Ensembl IDs |
| Slow CPU inference | Block mask compilation overhead | Add `--disable-compile-block-mask` when using `--device cpu` |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L66-L86), [src/transcriptformer/cli/__init__.py](/src/transcriptformer/cli/__init__.py#L194-L210)

# Model Variants and Species Coverage



TranscriptFormer ships with **three pretrained model variants**, each trained on a progressively broader phylogenetic scope of single-cell RNA-seq data. Choosing the right variant is the first—and most impactful—decision you'll make when using TranscriptFormer, because the variant determines which species' genes are present in the model's vocabulary and, consequently, which organisms you can run inference on without additional steps.

## The Three Variants at a Glance

The variant names follow a biological naming convention that directly signals their species coverage. Here's how they compare:

| Variant | Phylogenetic Scope | Typical Use Case | Checkpoint Directory |
|---|---|---|---|
| **tf-sapiens** | *Homo sapiens* (human only) | Human cell atlas analysis, clinical single-cell data | `checkpoints/tf_sapiens/` |
| **tf-exemplar** | Key model organisms (human, mouse, and select mammals) | Cross-species analysis between well-studied organisms | `checkpoints/tf_exemplar/` |
| **tf-metazoa** | Broad metazoan (animal) kingdom coverage | Multi-species studies, evolutionary comparisons, non-model organisms | `checkpoints/tf_metazoa/` |

Each variant is a complete, self-contained model bundle that includes trained weights, a gene vocabulary, and the pretrained protein embeddings needed for inference. You download them using the artifact download CLI:

```bash
# Download a single variant
transcriptformer download-artifacts tf-sapiens

# Or download all variants at once
transcriptformer download-artifacts all
```

The three options `tf-sapiens`, `tf-exemplar`, and `tf-metazoa` correspond to the three rows in the table above. There is also an `all-embeddings` option that downloads only the protein embedding files without model weights, which is useful for [Embedding Surgery for New Species](10-embedding-surgery-for-new-species).

Sources: [download_artifacts.py](/src/transcriptformer/cli/download_artifacts.py#L19-L50), [download_artifacts.py](/src/transcriptformer/cli/download_artifacts.py#L127-L164)

## How Variants Differ: Vocabulary and Embeddings

The fundamental difference between variants is **which genes are in the vocabulary**. TranscriptFormer represents each gene as a token whose initial embedding is derived from a pretrained ESM2 protein language model. The variant's vocabulary is the union of all ESM2 embedding files bundled in its checkpoint directory.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["ESM2 Protein Embeddings<br/>(per species)"] --> B["construct_gene_embeddings()"]
    B --> C["Gene Vocabulary Dict<br/>gene_name → token_index"]
    B --> D["Embedding Matrix<br/>[vocab_size × emb_dim]"]
    C --> E["GeneVocab Dataclass"]
    D --> F["PretrainedEmbeddings Module"]
    E --> G["TranscriptFormer Model"]
    F --> G

    style A fill:#e8f4e8,stroke:#2d7a2d
    style G fill:#dce6f7,stroke:#2d4d9e
```

When the model initializes, it calls `construct_gene_embeddings()` which reads all ESM2 mapping files listed in the checkpoint's `config.json`, concatenates them into a single embedding matrix, and builds a dictionary mapping every gene name to a unique integer index. Special tokens—`[START]`, `[END]`, `[PAD]`, `[CELL]`, `[RD]`, and `unknown`—are prepended to the vocabulary at indices 0–6. This means **the gene vocabulary size, and therefore the embedding matrix dimensions, differ across variants**.

> [!TIP]
> During inference, genes not present in the model's vocabulary are silently filtered out when `filter_to_vocabs: true` (the default). If your data contains many genes outside the vocabulary, you may lose significant signal. Choose the variant with the broadest coverage that matches your data, or use embedding surgery to extend it.

Sources: [vocab.py](/src/transcriptformer/tokenizer/vocab.py#L1-L116), [model.py](/src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L55-L89), [layers.py](/src/transcriptformer/model/layers.py#L299-L342)

## Variant Architecture Parameters

All three variants share the same architectural template—a Flex Attention Transformer Encoder with a count decoder head—but may differ in scale parameters. The key dimensions that can vary between checkpoints are:

| Parameter | Description | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `num_layers` | Number of transformer layers | Depth of the model; more layers capture more complex gene-gene interactions |
| `num_heads` | Number of attention heads | Granularity of multi-head attention |
| `model_dim` | Feed-forward hidden dimension | Capacity of each layer's MLP |
| `embed_dim` | Embedding dimension | Size of the projected gene representation |
| `seq_len` | Maximum sequence length | Maximum number of gene tokens per cell |

These values are stored in each checkpoint's `config.json` and are loaded automatically at inference time—you never need to specify them manually. When the inference script runs, it reads the checkpoint config, merges it with your CLI overrides, and instantiates the model with the correct dimensions.

Sources: [dataclasses.py](/src/transcriptformer/data/dataclasses.py#L18-L64), [inference.py](/src/transcriptformer/model/inference.py#L49-L86)

## Species Coverage and Data Compatibility

The practical question is: **which variant should I use for my data?** The answer depends on the organism(s) in your AnnData files. TranscriptFormer identifies genes by Ensembl ID (the `gene_col_name` defaults to `"ensembl_id"`), and only genes matching the variant's vocabulary will be retained during inference.

The test data included in the repository provides a concrete signal about validated species:

| Test File | Species | Variant Compatibility |
|---|---|---|
| `human_val.h5ad` | *Homo sapiens* | tf-sapiens ✓, tf-exemplar ✓, tf-metazoa ✓ |
| `mouse_val.h5ad` | *Mus musculus* | tf-exemplar ✓, tf-metazoa ✓ |
| `chicken_val.h5ad` | *Gallus gallus* | tf-metazoa ✓ |

The **tf-sapiens** variant is the most specialized—it covers only human genes. The **tf-exemplar** variant extends coverage to include key model organisms like mouse. The **tf-metazoa** variant has the broadest coverage, encompassing diverse species across the animal kingdom including chicken and other non-mammalian organisms.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Coverage Scope"
        S["🧬 tf-sapiens<br/>Human"]
        E["🧬 tf-exemplar<br/>Human + Mouse<br/>+ key mammals"]
        M["🧬 tf-metazoa<br/>Broad animal kingdom"]
    end
    S -.-> E -.-> M

    style S fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#856404
    style E fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724
    style M fill:#d1ecf1,stroke:#0c5460
```

> [!TIP]
> If you're working with a species not covered by any variant, don't despair—TranscriptFormer supports **embedding surgery**, which lets you swap in new protein embeddings for your target organism while keeping the trained transformer weights intact. See [Embedding Surgery for New Species](10-embedding-surgery-for-new-species) for the full walkthrough.

Sources: [inference_config.yaml](/src/transcriptformer/cli/conf/inference_config.yaml#L26-L29), [dataclasses.py](/src/transcriptformer/data/dataclasses.py#L67-L148)

## Downloading and Selecting a Variant

To run inference, you need both the model weights and the variant-specific vocabulary files. The download process extracts everything into a checkpoint directory with this structure:

```
checkpoints/
├── tf_sapiens/
│   ├── model_weights.pt
│   ├── config.json
│   └── vocabs/
│       ├── esm2_mappings/    # Protein embeddings for human genes
│       └── *_vocab.json      # Auxiliary vocabularies
├── tf_exemplar/
│   ├── model_weights.pt
│   ├── config.json
│   └── vocabs/
│       ├── esm2_mappings/    # Protein embeddings for exemplar species
│       └── *_vocab.json
└── tf_metazoa/
    ├── model_weights.pt
    ├── config.json
    └── vocabs/
        ├── esm2_mappings/    # Protein embeddings for metazoan species
        └── *_vocab.json
```

Point the `model.checkpoint_path` argument to the appropriate directory when running inference:

```bash
# Example: using the metazoa variant
transcriptformer inference \
  model.checkpoint_path=./checkpoints/tf_metazoa \
  model.inference_config.data_files.0=my_data.h5ad
```

The `all_embeddings` download option provides the standalone protein embedding files used by the embedding surgery mechanism, allowing you to extend any variant to cover new species without retraining.

Sources: [download_artifacts.py](/src/transcriptformer/cli/download_artifacts.py#L56-L122), [inference.py](/src/transcriptformer/cli/inference.py#L38-L52)

- **To extend a variant to a new species**: Read [Embedding Surgery for New Species](10-embedding-surgery-for-new-species) for the step-by-step procedure.

# Architecture Overview



TranscriptFormer is an autoregressive transformer model that learns biologically meaningful representations of single-cell transcriptomic data by predicting gene tokens and their expression counts. Unlike language models that process sequential text, TranscriptFormer operates on **unordered sets of gene–count pairs**, using count-conditioned attention biases and causal masking to model the joint distribution of gene identity and expression within a cell. The architecture fuses pretrained protein embeddings with a Flex Attention transformer encoder and a count decoder head, trained end-to-end with a Zero-Truncated Poisson loss that respects the strictly-positive nature of observed expression counts.

![Model Overview](https://github.com/czi-ai/transcriptformer/blob/main/assets/model_overview.png?raw=true)

Sources: [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L39-L40), [model_overview.png](assets/model_overview.png)

## System Architecture at a Glance

The codebase is organized into four primary subsystems—**tokenization**, **data loading**, **model**, and **inference**—each with a clear boundary of responsibility. The model subsystem is the architectural core, containing the transformer encoder, embedding layers, decoder heads, loss functions, attention masks, and the embedding surgery module. The inference subsystem orchestrates the full pipeline: loading vocabularies and embeddings, constructing the model, performing optional embedding surgery, and dispatching prediction via PyTorch Lightning's `Trainer`.

```
src/transcriptformer/
├── cli/                        # Command-line interface
│   ├── conf/inference_config.yaml
│   ├── download_artifacts.py
│   ├── download_data.py
│   └── inference.py
├── data/                       # Data subsystem
│   ├── dataclasses.py          # Config & batch dataclasses
│   └── dataloader.py           # AnnDataset, filtering, preprocessing
├── datasets.py                 # Public dataset download helpers
├── model/                      # Model subsystem (core)
│   ├── model.py                # Transcriptformer & ESM2CE classes
│   ├── layers.py               # Encoder, attention, embeddings, decoder
│   ├── losses.py               # ZTP NLL & CrossEntropy losses
│   ├── masks.py                # Causal & padding mask factories
│   ├── embedding_surgery.py    # Cross-species embedding swap
│   └── inference.py            # Full inference orchestration
├── tokenizer/                  # Tokenization subsystem
│   ├── tokenizer.py            # BatchGeneTokenizer, BatchObsTokenizer
│   └── vocab.py                # Vocabulary construction & loading
└── utils/                      # Shared utilities
    └── utils.py
```

Sources: [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L1-L36), [layers.py](src/transcriptformer/model/layers.py#L1-L12), [dataclasses.py](src/transcriptformer/data/dataclasses.py#L1-L10)

## End-to-End Data Flow

The following diagram traces the complete forward pass of the `Transcriptformer` model—from raw gene–count inputs through embedding, attention, decoding, and loss computation. This is the central execution path that ties all subsystems together.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Input["Input Processing"]
        A["Gene Token Indices<br/>(batch, seq_len)"] --> B["Right-Shift Tokens<br/>Prepend [START]"]
        C["Gene Counts<br/>(batch, seq_len)"] --> D["Right-Shift Counts<br/>Prepend 1"]
        E["Aux Token Indices<br/>(e.g., assay)"] --> F["Aux Embeddings<br/>(nn.Embedding per aux field)"]
    end

    subgraph Embedding["Embedding Layer"]
        B --> G["PretrainedEmbeddings<br/>Frozen ESM2 + MLP projection"]
        D --> H["log1p(counts + eps)<br/>Log-count transform"]
    end

    subgraph Sequence["Sequence Assembly"]
        G --> I["Concat: [aux_emb | gene_emb]<br/>(batch, aux_len+seq_len, embed_dim)"]
        F --> I
        H --> J["Concat: [ones | log_counts]<br/>(batch, aux_len+seq_len)"]
    end

    subgraph Attention["Flex Attention Encoder"]
        I --> K["TranscriptEncoder<br/>N × FlexAttnTransformerLayer"]
        J --> L["score_mod:<br/>log_count bias + softcap"]
        K --> L
        M["block_mask:<br/>causal ∧ pad mask"] --> K
    end

    subgraph Output["Output Heads"]
        K --> N["Gene Output<br/>(remove aux prefix)"]
        N --> O["CountDecoderHead<br/>Skip-connect: cat[gene_out, gene_emb]<br/>→ MLP → link_fn(softmax/sigmoid/...)"]
        N --> P["Gene ID Head<br/>MLP → vocab logits<br/>(optional, weight > 0)"]
        N --> Q["Cell Embeddings<br/>mean_pool(gene_out, mask)"]
        N --> R["Contextual Gene Emb<br/>Per-gene output vectors"]
    end

    subgraph Loss["Loss Computation"]
        O --> S["ZTP NLL Loss<br/>(zero-truncated Poisson)"]
        P --> T["CrossEntropy Loss<br/>+ optional logit softcap"]
    end
```

Sources: [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L251-L383), [layers.py](src/transcriptformer/model/layers.py#L146-L223), [losses.py](src/transcriptformer/model/losses.py#L47-L129)

## Core Architectural Components

### Pretrained Gene Embeddings

Each gene is represented by a **frozen** pretrained protein embedding (derived from ESM-2), projected through a learned 2-layer MLP into the model's embedding dimension. The `PretrainedEmbeddings` module wraps an `nn.Embedding.from_pretrained` layer with `freeze=True`, then passes embeddings through an MLP with LayerNorm and dropout. This design preserves the rich biological semantics captured by the protein language model while allowing the projection to adapt to the transcriptomic domain.

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Source embeddings | ESM-2 protein embeddings |
| Freeze status | Frozen (`requires_grad=False`) |
| Projection | 2-layer MLP with LayerNorm + ReLU + Dropout |
| Normalization | LayerNorm on intermediate representations |
| Special tokens | Randomly initialized (seeded) |

Sources: [layers.py](src/transcriptformer/model/layers.py#L355-L394), [vocab.py](src/transcriptformer/tokenizer/vocab.py#L13-L57)

### Flex Attention Transformer Encoder

The `TranscriptEncoder` stacks `N` identical `FlexAttnTransformerLayer` modules, each following a **pre-norm** architecture: `LayerNorm → Self-Attention + Residual → LayerNorm → Feed-Forward + Residual`. The critical design departure from standard transformers is the use of PyTorch's `flex_attention`, which accepts a `score_mod` function and a `block_mask`—enabling two architectural innovations:

1. **Count-conditioned attention bias**: The `score_mod` function injects `log(1 + count)` as an additive bias to attention scores for positions where the query index exceeds the key index. This means each gene's influence on subsequent predictions is weighted by its expression level—a high-count gene "speaks louder" in the attention mechanism.

2. **Causal + padding block mask**: A composite `block_mask` is constructed by AND-ing a causal mask (positions can only attend to themselves and prior positions) with a padding mask (masking out `[PAD]` tokens). The `block_mask` format enables efficient sparse attention computation via `torch.compile`.

> [!TIP]
> The `score_mod` closure captures `log_counts` at forward time, so the attention bias dynamically reflects the actual expression profile of each cell in the batch—not a static positional encoding.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| `embed_dim` | Dimension of input/output embeddings |
| `num_heads` | Number of attention heads |
| `model_dim` | Feed-forward hidden dimension |
| `nlayers` | Number of transformer layers |
| `activation` | GELU (default), ReLU, or SiLU |
| `compile_attention` | Whether to `torch.compile` flex_attention |
| `attn_bias` / `fw_bias` | Linear layer biases (default: False) |

Sources: [layers.py](src/transcriptformer/model/layers.py#L24-L223), [masks.py](src/transcriptformer/model/masks.py#L1-L16), [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L205-L215)

### Count Decoder Head

The `CountDecoderHead` predicts the rate parameter μ of the expression distribution for each gene position. It receives a **skip-connected input** formed by concatenating the transformer's gene output with the original (non-right-shifted) gene embeddings—doubling the effective input dimension to `2 × embed_dim`. This skip connection allows the decoder to condition on both the contextualized representation and the raw gene identity when predicting expression.

Internally, the head applies a 2-layer MLP (with hidden dimension = `model_dim / 4`) that outputs a scalar logit per position, adds an optional **gene-specific bias** via `nn.Embedding(vocab_size, 1)`, then applies a link function. The default `softmax` link normalizes the output across all gene positions and scales by total cell counts—effectively predicting a proportion of the total expression budget allocated to each gene.

| Link Function | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `softmax` | Proportional allocation, scaled by total counts |
| `sigmoid` | Bounded [0, 1] per gene |
| `softplus` | Smooth positive activation |
| `exp` | Unbounded positive |
| `relu` | Clipped at zero |
| `linear` | Identity (no transformation) |

Sources: [layers.py](src/transcriptformer/model/layers.py#L249-L353), [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L140-L148)

### Gene ID Prediction Head (Auxiliary)

When `gene_id_loss_weight > 0`, an auxiliary `MLP` head is trained to predict the identity of the next gene token from the transformer output. This provides an additional supervision signal that encourages the model to learn gene co-expression patterns. The head maps from `embed_dim` through a hidden layer to `vocab_size` logits, with optional logit softcapping via `logit_softcap` to prevent extreme confidence.

Sources: [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L150-L170), [losses.py](src/transcriptformer/model/losses.py#L23-L44)

## Configuration Architecture

The model is configured through a hierarchy of dataclasses that decouple architectural decisions (`ModelConfig`), data processing rules (`DataConfig`), loss parameters (`LossConfig`), and inference behavior (`InferenceConfig`). These are assembled at instantiation time and stored as attributes on the `Transcriptformer` module.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class ModelConfig {
        +embed_dim : int
        +num_heads : int
        +num_layers : int
        +model_dim : int
        +dropout : float
        +activation : str
        +mu_link_fn : str
        +softcap : int
        +seq_len : int
        +block_len : int
    }
    class DataConfig {
        +gene_col_name : str
        +clip_counts : bool
        +filter_to_vocabs : bool
        +normalize_to_scale : bool
        +sort_genes : bool
        +randomize_genes : bool
    }
    class LossConfig {
        +gene_id_loss_weight : float
        +softplus_approx : bool
    }
    class InferenceConfig {
        +batch_size : int
        +output_keys : list
        +emb_type : str
        +num_gpus : int
        +device : str
        +"pretrained_embedding : list[]"
    }
    class Transcriptformer {
        +model_config : ModelConfig
        +data_config : DataConfig
        +loss_config : LossConfig
        +inference_config : InferenceConfig
        +forward()
        +inference()
    }
    Transcriptformer --> ModelConfig
    Transcriptformer --> DataConfig
    Transcriptformer --> LossConfig
    Transcriptformer --> InferenceConfig
```

Sources: [dataclasses.py](src/transcriptformer/data/dataclasses.py#L14-L73), [dataclasses.py](src/transcriptformer/data/dataclasses.py#L152-L209)

## Model Variants

The codebase implements two model variants that share the same configuration infrastructure but differ in their forward pass:

| Variant | Class | Forward Pass Behavior | Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Transcriptformer** | `Transcriptformer` | Full autoregressive pass: right-shift tokens → pretrained embeddings → transformer encoder → count decoder + gene ID head | Training & inference |
| **ESM2-CE** | `ESM2CE` | Embedding-only pass: raw ESM2 embeddings (no MLP projection, no transformer) → mean pool → cell/contextual gene embeddings | Baseline embedding extraction |

The `ESM2CE` variant is a lightweight baseline that bypasses the transformer entirely, returning the frozen pretrained protein embeddings directly (via `embed_only=True`). It exists to evaluate how much the transformer encoder adds beyond the pretrained protein embeddings alone.

Sources: [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L482-L527), [inference.py](src/transcriptformer/model/inference.py#L51-L61)

## Embedding Surgery for Cross-Species Transfer

A distinctive architectural feature is **embedding surgery**—the ability to swap the gene embedding layer at inference time to support species not seen during training. The `change_embedding_layer` function preserves special token embeddings from the trained model, concatenates them with new species' pretrained protein embeddings, reconstructs the `nn.Embedding` layer, and updates the vocabulary mapping. This enables zero-shot transfer to novel organisms without retraining.

> [!TIP]
> Embedding surgery is triggered by setting `pretrained_embedding` in the inference config. The model's vocabulary and embedding matrix are mutated in-place, so the same model object can serve multiple species sequentially.

Sources: [embedding_surgery.py](src/transcriptformer/model/embedding_surgery.py#L7-L79), [inference.py](src/transcriptformer/model/inference.py#L111-L118)

Now that you understand the overall architecture, explore each component in depth:

- **[Pretrained Protein Embeddings](5-pretrained-protein-embeddings)** — How ESM-2 embeddings are extracted, stored, and projected into the model
- **[Flex Attention Transformer Encoder](6-flex-attention-transformer-encoder)** — The count-conditioned attention mechanism and block masking in detail

# Pretrained Protein Embeddings



TranscriptFormer replaces the traditional learned gene embedding layer with **pretrained protein language model embeddings** from ESM-2 (Evolutionary Scale Modeling). Rather than learning gene representations from scratch on transcriptomic data alone, each gene is anchored to a fixed vector derived from the amino acid sequence of its encoded protein — injecting rich evolutionary and structural information into the model before a single cell is seen. This design choice is the foundation of TranscriptFormer's cross-species transfer capability and its strong zero-shot performance on unseen organisms.

## Why Protein Embeddings?

Single-cell transcriptomic models face a fundamental vocabulary problem: genes are typically treated as opaque categorical tokens whose relationships must be discovered entirely from expression co-variation. This forces the model to re-learn what biology already knows — that BRCA1 and BRCA2 share functional pathways, that orthologs across species carry conserved structure, and that protein sequence encodes function. ESM-2 embeddings, pretrained on millions of protein sequences via masked language modeling, capture exactly these evolutionary and structural regularities. By freezing these embeddings at the input layer, TranscriptFormer ensures that every gene's initial representation already encodes its protein-level biology, and the transformer encoder only needs to learn **how** these proteins interact within the context of a cell's expression profile.

Sources: [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L110-L117), [protein_embedding.py](preprocess/protein_embedding.py#L70-L143)

## Embedding Generation Pipeline

The preprocessing pipeline converts raw protein sequences from Ensembl into gene-level embedding matrices stored in HDF5 format. The entire flow — from FASTA download to frozen embedding tensor — is orchestrated by `protein_embedding.py`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Ensembl FTP<br/>Protein FASTA"] -->|"Download & decompress"| B["FASTA File<br/>(per species)"]
    B -->|"Parse headers<br/>Extract gene IDs"| C["Deduplicated<br/>Gene → Sequence Map"]
    C -->|"Clean sequences<br/>(replace * with &lt;unk&gt;)"| D["Tokenized<br/>Protein Sequences"]
    D -->|"ESM-2 Forward Pass<br/>(layer 33 or 48)"| E["Per-Residue<br/>Representations"]
    E -->|"Mean pool<br/>across residues"| F["Per-Isoform<br/>Embeddings"]
    F -->|"Average across<br/>isoforms per gene"| G["Gene-Level<br/>Embedding Vector"]
    G -->|"Save as HDF5"| H["{organism}_gene.h5<br/>d=2560 or d=5120"]
```

### ESM-2 Model Selection

Two ESM-2 model variants are supported, selectable via the `--use_large_model` flag:

| Property | ESM-2 3B (default) | ESM-2 15B (`--use_large_model`) |
|---|---|---|
| Model ID | `esm2_t36_3B_UR50D` | `esm2_t48_15B_UR50D` |
| Parameters | 3 billion | 15 billion |
| Layers | 36 | 48 |
| Representation layer | 33 | 48 |
| Embedding dimension | 2560 | 5120 |
| Output suffix | `{organism}_gene.h5` | `{organism}_gene_large.h5` |
| TranscriptFormer default | ✅ | ❌ |
| UCE default | ❌ | ✅ |

The pipeline extracts representations from the penultimate layer (layer 33 for the 3B model), mean-pools across all residues in each protein sequence to produce a fixed-length vector per isoform, and then averages across all isoforms belonging to the same gene to yield a single gene-level embedding. This isoform-averaging ensures that alternative splicing does not fragment a gene's representation.

> [!TIP]
> When generating embeddings for a new species, always use the same ESM-2 variant that your target TranscriptFormer checkpoint was trained with. Mixing the 3B-generated embeddings into a model trained on 15B embeddings (or vice versa) will produce dimension mismatches and semantically meaningless projections.

Sources: [protein_embedding.py](preprocess/protein_embedding.py#L70-L143), [protein_embedding.py](preprocess/protein_embedding.py#L146-L257)

### Supported Species and FASTA Manifest

The `fasta_manifest_pep.json` file maps organism keys to their Ensembl protein FASTA download URLs. As of the current release, **19 species** are supported, spanning mammals, birds, fish, amphibians, invertebrates, and even coral:

| Clade | Organism Key | Common Name |
|---|---|---|
| Primate | `homo_sapiens` | Human |
| Primate | `pan_troglodytes` | Chimpanzee |
| Primate | `gorilla_gorilla` | Gorilla |
| Primate | `macaca_mulatta` | Rhesus macaque |
| Primate | `callithrix_jacchus` | Marmoset |
| Primate | `microcebus_murinus` | Mouse lemur |
| Rodent | `mus_musculus` | Mouse |
| Rodent | `rattus_norvegicus` | Rat |
| Rodent | `heterocephalus_glaber` | Naked mole-rat |
| Ungulate | `sus_scrofa` | Pig |
| Lagomorph | `oryctolagus_cuniculus` | Rabbit |
| Bird | `gallus_gallus` | Chicken |
| Fish | `danio_rerio` | Zebrafish |
| Amphibian | `xenopus_tropicalis` | Frog |
| Monotreme | `ornithorhynchus_anatinus` | Platypus |
| Marsupial | `monodelphis_domestica` | Opossum |
| Invertebrate | `drosophila_melanogaster` | Fruit fly |
| Invertebrate | `stylophora_pistillata` | Coral |
| Jawless fish | `petromyzon_marinus` | Sea lamprey |

To add a new species, append an entry to the manifest with the appropriate Ensembl FTP URL for the `.pep.all.fa.gz` file. The pipeline will automatically download, parse, embed, and save the gene-level embeddings.

Sources: [fasta_manifest_pep.json](preprocess/fasta_manifest_pep.json#L1-L63), [README.md](preprocess/README.md#L86-L110)

### Output Format and Storage

Embeddings are saved in HDF5 format with a two-level structure: a `keys` dataset containing gene identifier strings, and an `arrays` group containing one dataset per gene. The utility function `load_from_hdf5` decodes byte-string keys and returns a Python dictionary mapping gene names to numpy arrays.

```python
# HDF5 structure
# ├── keys: array of byte-string gene IDs (e.g., b"ENSG00000139618")
# └── arrays/
#     ├── ENSG00000139618: float32 array, shape (2560,)
#     ├── ENSG00000141510: float32 array, shape (2560,)
#     └── ...
```

Sources: [utils.py](src/transcriptformer/utils/utils.py#L13-L45), [protein_embedding.py](preprocess/protein_embedding.py#L23-L33)

## From Embedding Files to Model Layer

The path from HDF5 files on disk to a frozen embedding layer inside the model involves three distinct stages: loading and deduplication, vocabulary construction, and projection via the `PretrainedEmbeddings` module.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Stage 1: Load & Deduplicate"
        A["{organism}_gene.h5"] -->|"load_embeddings()"| B["Dict[gene_name → vector]"]
        B -->|"Deduplicate genes"| C["Unique gene list + vectors"]
    end
    subgraph "Stage 2: Vocabulary Construction"
        C -->|"Add special tokens<br/>(random init)"| D["Full vocab dict<br/>+ concatenated matrix"]
        D -->|"construct_gene_embeddings()"| E["gene_vocab_dict + emb_matrix"]
    end
    subgraph "Stage 3: Model Integration"
        E -->|"PretrainedEmbeddings"| F["nn.Embedding.from_pretrained<br/>(frozen)"]
        F -->|"2-layer MLP<br/>(trainable)"| G["Output dim = embed_dim<br/>(e.g., 2048)"]
    end
```

### Vocabulary Construction

The `construct_gene_embeddings` function in `vocab.py` is the bridge between raw embedding files and the model. It accepts a list of HDF5 file paths, loads each one, concatenates the gene names and vectors, deduplicates any overlapping genes (logging a warning for each duplicate removed), and then prepends **special token embeddings** — randomly initialized vectors for `[PAD]`, `[START]`, `[END]`, `[RD]`, `[CELL]`, `unknown`, and `_SEP_`. The resulting `gene_vocab_dict` maps each gene name and special token to a unique integer index, while the `emb_matrix` is a single numpy array whose row indices correspond exactly to those vocabulary indices.

The random initialization of special tokens uses a fixed seed (`random_seed=42`) for reproducibility. This is critical because special tokens serve structural roles in the model (padding, sequence boundaries, cell-level conditioning) and should not carry protein-level semantic information.

Sources: [vocab.py](src/transcriptformer/tokenizer/vocab.py#L13-L57), [vocab.py](src/transcriptformer/tokenizer/vocab.py#L88-L95)

### The PretrainedEmbeddings Module

The `PretrainedEmbeddings` class is the model-level component that wraps the frozen ESM-2 embeddings and projects them into the model's internal dimensionality. Its architecture is deliberately simple:

| Component | Trainable | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `nn.Embedding.from_pretrained` | ❌ Frozen | Lookup ESM-2 vectors by gene token index |
| `MLP` (2-layer) | ✅ Trainable | Project from ESM-2 dim (2560) to `embed_dim` (2048) |
| LayerNorm in MLP | ✅ Trainable | Normalize projected representations |
| Dropout in MLP | ✅ Trainable | Regularization during training |

The freezing behavior is controlled by the `freeze` parameter (default `True`), which sets `requires_grad = False` on the embedding weight matrix. The MLP projection uses ReLU activation between layers and LayerNorm before the output, with dropout applied for regularization. The `forward` method supports an `embed_only` flag that bypasses the MLP and returns raw ESM-2 vectors — this is used by the `ESM2CE` variant for direct embedding extraction.

> [!TIP]
> The MLP projection is the only trainable component in the embedding layer. If you are fine-tuning TranscriptFormer on a new dataset, the ESM-2 vectors remain fixed while the projection adapts to the model's internal representation space. This preserves the cross-species semantic structure while allowing domain-specific adaptation.

Sources: [layers.py](src/transcriptformer/model/layers.py#L355-L394), [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L110-L117)

## Model Integration: How Embeddings Flow Through TranscriptFormer

Inside the `Transcriptformer` model, gene embeddings participate in two distinct pathways during the forward pass. The `get_gene_embeddings` method produces both **right-shifted embeddings** (conditioned on previous tokens, for autoregressive input to the transformer) and **non-shifted embeddings** (used for the skip-connection in the count decoder). This dual pathway means each gene's ESM-2 representation influences both the self-attention computation and the final expression prediction.

```python
# Simplified flow from model.py forward()
right_shifted_gene_embeddings, gene_embeddings = self.get_gene_embeddings(batch)

# Path 1: Transformer input (autoregressive conditioning)
transformer_output = self.transformer_encoder(x=right_shifted_gene_embeddings, ...)

# Path 2: Skip connection to count decoder (concatenation)
conditioned_output = torch.cat([gene_output, gene_embeddings], dim=-1)
result["mu"] = self.mu(gene_output=conditioned_output, gene_tokens=gene_token_indices, ...)
```

The concatenation of transformer output with the original ESM-2-projected embeddings (`conditioned_output`) doubles the effective dimensionality at the count decoder input, allowing the model to simultaneously access the cell-contextualized representation and the original protein-level identity of each gene.

Sources: [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L187-L196), [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L287-L369)

## The ESM2CE Variant: Embeddings Without a Transformer

TranscriptFormer includes a lightweight variant called `ESM2CE` that bypasses the transformer encoder entirely. In this mode, `forward()` calls `self.gene_embeddings(gene_token_indices, embed_only=True)`, returning the raw ESM-2 embeddings (after the frozen lookup but before the MLP projection) as cell or contextual gene embeddings. This variant serves as a baseline to quantify the value added by the transformer encoder on top of pretrained protein embeddings alone.

Sources: [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L482-L527)

## Embedding Surgery: Extending to New Species

When applying a pretrained TranscriptFormer model to a species not seen during training, the embedding layer must be replaced with one covering the new organism's gene vocabulary. The `change_embedding_layer` function in `embedding_surgery.py` performs this operation by: (1) extracting the learned special token embeddings from the existing model, (2) constructing new gene embeddings from HDF5 files for the target species, (3) concatenating the preserved special token embeddings with the new gene embeddings, and (4) updating both the `nn.Embedding` layer and the `gene_vocab` dictionary. This preserves the model's learned behavior on structural tokens while enabling it to process entirely new gene sets.

For the full procedure and configuration, see [Embedding Surgery for New Species](10-embedding-surgery-for-new-species).

Sources: [embedding_surgery.py](src/transcriptformer/model/embedding_surgery.py#L7-L79)

## Key Design Decisions and Trade-offs

| Design Choice | Rationale | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **Freeze ESM-2 embeddings** | Preserves cross-species protein semantics; prevents catastrophic forgetting of evolutionary information | Cannot adapt gene representations to transcriptomic context at the embedding level |
| **MLP projection (trainable)** | Allows the model to learn an optimal mapping from ESM-2 space to model space | Adds parameters; projection must be relearned during fine-tuning |
| **Mean-pool protein residues** | Produces fixed-length gene vectors regardless of protein length | Loses positional information within the protein sequence |
| **Average across isoforms** | One vector per gene regardless of alternative splicing | Collapses isoform-specific structural differences |
| **Random special token init** | Special tokens serve structural roles, not semantic ones | Slight sensitivity to random seed; mitigated by fixed seed |
| **Layer 33 extraction (3B)** | Penultimate layer balances high-level semantics with task-relevant features | Not the final layer; may miss some task-specific fine-tuning signal |

Sources: [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L110-L117), [layers.py](src/transcriptformer/model/layers.py#L355-L394), [protein_embedding.py](preprocess/protein_embedding.py#L122-L128), [vocab.py](src/transcriptformer/tokenizer/vocab.py#L53-L57)

## Next Steps

- Understand how the projected embeddings are processed by the transformer: [Flex Attention Transformer Encoder](6-flex-attention-transformer-encoder)
- See how gene tokens and counts are prepared for embedding lookup: [Gene Tokenizer and Vocabulary](11-gene-tokenizer-and-vocabulary)
- Learn how to extend embeddings to new species at inference time: [Embedding Surgery for New Species](10-embedding-surgery-for-new-species)

# Flex Attention Transformer Encoder



The Flex Attention Transformer Encoder is the computational core of TranscriptFormer — a stack of pre-norm transformer layers that leverages PyTorch's `flex_attention` primitive to implement two domain-specific modifications to standard self-attention: **count-informed attention bias** (via `score_mod`) and **causal padding-aware block masking** (via `block_mask`). Together, these mechanisms allow the encoder to reason about gene expression magnitude directly within the attention computation while maintaining efficient autoregressive masking over variable-length, padded gene sequences.

## Architectural Overview

The encoder is composed of three nested modules, each with a distinct responsibility. `MultiHeadSelfFlexAttn` implements the low-level attention mechanism with flex attention's `score_mod` and `block_mask` hooks. `FlexAttnTransformerLayer` wraps that attention with a pre-norm residual block and a feed-forward network. `TranscriptEncoder` stacks N identical layers and threads the shared `score_mod` and `block_mask` through every layer. The following diagram captures these relationships and the data flow from model-level orchestration down through each component.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph Transcriptformer["Transcriptformer (LightningModule)"]
        A["_score_mod_factory(log_counts)"] -->|score_mod| TE
        B["create_block_mask(pad_mask ∧ causal_mask)"] -->|block_mask| TE
    end

    subgraph TE["TranscriptEncoder"]
        direction TB
        L1["FlexAttnTransformerLayer 1"]
        L2["FlexAttnTransformerLayer 2"]
        LN["FlexAttnTransformerLayer N"]
        L1 --> L2 --> LN
    end

    subgraph Layer["FlexAttnTransformerLayer (each)"]
        direction TB
        PN1["Pre-Norm (LayerNorm)"] --> SA["MultiHeadSelfFlexAttn"]
        SA -->|+ residual| RS1["Residual Add"]
        RS1 --> PN2["Pre-Norm (LayerNorm)"]
        PN2 --> FFN["FFN: Linear → Act → Dropout → Linear"]
        FFN -->|+ residual| RS2["Residual Add"]
    end

    subgraph MHSA["MultiHeadSelfFlexAttn"]
        direction TB
        QKV["Linear projections (Q, K, V)"] --> FA["flex_attention(score_mod, block_mask)"]
        FA --> CAT["Concat heads"] --> OL["Output Linear"]
    end

    TE --> Layer
    SA --> MHSA
```

Sources: [layers.py](src/transcriptformer/model/layers.py#L27-L98), [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L218-L246), [masks.py](src/transcriptformer/model/masks.py#L1-L17)

## MultiHeadSelfFlexAttn: The Attention Primitive

`MultiHeadSelfFlexAttn` replaces the standard scaled dot-product attention with PyTorch's `torch.nn.attention.flex_attention.flex_attention`, which exposes two hooks for domain-specific customization:

- **`score_mod`**: A closure invoked element-wise on the attention score matrix, enabling additive bias or multiplicative scaling before softmax.
- **`block_mask**: A structured block-sparse mask that determines which (query, key) blocks participate in attention, compiled into an efficient sparse representation.

The module performs the classic multi-head attention factorization — projecting input into Q, K, V via three separate linear layers (each `d_model → d_model`, no bias by default), reshaping into `(batch, heads, seq, d_k)`, applying flex attention, concatenating heads, and projecting back through a fourth linear layer. The key architectural choice is that `score_mod` and `block_mask` are **not** stored as module parameters but are instead **injected at forward time**, allowing the same attention module to serve both training (causal + count-biased) and embedding extraction (bidirectional + count-biased) modes without re-initialization.

> [!TIP]
> The `compile_attention` flag controls whether `flex_attention` is wrapped in `torch.compile(fullgraph=True)`. Compilation fuses the attention kernel and score modification into a single GPU kernel, which is critical for performance with block-sparse masks. Disabling it is useful for debugging but incurs significant runtime overhead on large sequences.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `d_model` | `int` | required | Model dimension (must be divisible by `nheads`) |
| `nheads` | `int` | required | Number of attention heads; determines `d_k = d_model // nheads` |
| `bias` | `bool` | `False` | Whether to include bias in the Q/K/V/output linear layers |
| `compile_attention` | `bool` | `True` | Wrap `flex_attention` in `torch.compile(fullgraph=True)` |

Sources: [layers.py](src/transcriptformer/model/layers.py#L27-L98)

## FlexAttnTransformerLayer: Pre-Norm Residual Block

Each transformer layer follows the **pre-norm** architecture — layer normalization is applied *before* the attention and feed-forward sublayers rather than after. This ordering, denoted as "pre-norm is the new norm" in the codebase, stabilizes training for deep transformers by ensuring the residual path carries gradients with unit scale. The forward computation for each layer is:

```
x = LayerNorm(x)
x = MultiHeadSelfFlexAttn(x, score_mod, block_mask) + x    # residual 1
x = LayerNorm(x)
x = Linear2(Dropout(Activation(Linear1(x)))) + x           # residual 2
```

The feed-forward network is a two-layer MLP with configurable hidden dimension (`dim_fw`), activation function, and dropout. The activation is selectable among `relu`, `gelu` (default), and `silu`. Notably, **bias is independently configurable** for both the attention linear layers (`attn_bias`) and the feed-forward layers (`fw_bias`), both defaulting to `False` — a common practice in modern transformer designs where LayerNorm absorbs the bias role.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `d_model` | `int` | required | Model dimension |
| `nhead` | `int` | required | Number of attention heads |
| `dim_fw` | `int` | `2048` | Feed-forward hidden dimension |
| `dropout` | `float` | `0.0` | Dropout rate applied after FFN activation |
| `fw_bias` | `bool` | `False` | Bias in feed-forward linear layers |
| `attn_bias` | `bool` | `False` | Bias in attention linear layers |
| `activation` | `str` | `"gelu"` | Activation function: `relu`, `gelu`, or `silu` |
| `compile_attention` | `bool` | `True` | Compile flex attention kernel |

Sources: [layers.py](src/transcriptformer/model/layers.py#L101-L189)

## TranscriptEncoder: Stacked Layers with Shared Masks

`TranscriptEncoder` is a thin container that instantiates `N` identical `FlexAttnTransformerLayer` modules and threads the same `score_mod` and `block_mask` through every layer during the forward pass. This design ensures that all layers respect the same causal and padding constraints, and that the count-informed bias is applied consistently at every depth.

```python
def forward(self, x, score_mod, block_mask):
    for layer in self.encoder_layers:
        x = layer(x, score_mod=score_mod, block_mask=block_mask)
    return x
```

The `score_mod` and `block_mask` are constructed externally (in `Transcriptformer.forward`) and passed in — the encoder has no internal knowledge of what they compute. This separation of concerns means the encoder is agnostic to whether it's running in autoregressive training mode, bidirectional embedding mode, or any future masking strategy.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `embed_dim` | `int` | required | Embedding / model dimension |
| `num_head` | `int` | required | Number of attention heads per layer |
| `nlayers` | `int` | required | Number of transformer layers |
| `model_dim` | `int` | `2048` | Feed-forward hidden dimension |
| `dropout` | `float` | `0.0` | Dropout rate |
| `activation` | `str` | `"gelu"` | Activation function |
| `attn_bias` | `bool` | `False` | Attention linear layer bias |
| `fw_bias` | `bool` | `False` | Feed-forward linear layer bias |
| `compile_attention` | `bool` | `True` | Compile flex attention kernel |

Sources: [layers.py](src/transcriptformer/model/layers.py#L192-L252)

## Score Modification: Count-Informed Attention Bias

The most domain-critical component of the flex attention encoder is the **score modification function**, which injects gene expression information directly into the attention computation. This is defined as a closure in `Transcriptformer._score_mod_factory`:

```python
def _score_mod_factory(self, log_counts, emb_mode=False):
    softcap = self.model_config.softcap
    def score_mod(score, b, h, q_idx, kv_idx):
        bias = log_counts[b, kv_idx] * ((q_idx > kv_idx) | emb_mode)
        score = score + bias
        if softcap > 0:
            score = logit_softcap(score, softcap)
        return score
    return score_mod
```

The function receives the raw attention `score` and the four coordinate indices `(b, h, q_idx, kv_idx)` and performs two operations:

**1. Log-Count Bias**: The expression level of the *key* gene (the gene being attended to) is added as an additive bias to the attention score. The log-transformed count `log1p(count + eps)` acts as a signal of how prominently a gene is expressed — highly expressed genes receive stronger attention. Critically, the bias is applied **only when `q_idx > kv_idx`** during autoregressive training (i.e., the query is to the right of the key), which means a gene can only attend to the expression levels of *previously seen* genes. When `emb_mode=True` (embedding extraction), the condition becomes unconditional — `(q_idx > kv_idx) | True` — allowing bidirectional count-informed attention for producing cell-level embeddings.

**2. Logit Softcapping**: When `softcap > 0` (default: 10), attention scores are bounded via the `logit_softcap` function, which applies `softcap * tanh(score / softcap)`. This prevents attention scores from growing unboundedly, which can destabilize training with large expression values. The softcapping is applied *after* the count bias, ensuring both the raw score and the bias contribution are jointly capped.

> [!TIP]
> The `emb_mode` flag is what transforms the encoder from an autoregressive predictor into a bidirectional embedding extractor. During training, the causal constraint (`q_idx > kv_idx`) prevents information leakage from future tokens. During inference for cell embeddings, setting `emb_mode=True` removes this constraint, allowing each gene to attend to all other genes' expression levels — producing richer, context-aware representations.

Sources: [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L218-L230), [losses.py](src/transcriptformer/model/losses.py#L24-L38)

## Block Mask: Causal + Padding-Aware Sparse Attention

The block mask is the second flex attention primitive, constructed by composing two mask factories via `torch.nn.attention.flex_attention.and_masks`:

```python
mask_mod = and_masks(pad_mask_factory(pad_mask), self.causal_mask)
```

**Padding Mask** (`pad_mask_factory`): This mask prevents attention to padded gene positions. It takes a boolean mask indicating which positions are valid (non-padded) for each batch element and returns `True` only when the key position (`kv_idx`) is valid. This ensures that padded genes — which carry no biological signal — do not receive or contribute attention weight.

**Causal Mask** (`causal_mask_factory`): This mask enforces the autoregressive property — each position can only attend to itself and earlier positions. The default factory (with `offset=0`) creates the standard lower-triangular mask where `q_idx >= kv_idx`. The factory supports configurable `start_row`, `start_col`, and `offset` parameters, though the default configuration uses none of these.

The composed mask is compiled into a block-sparse representation via `create_block_mask`, which partitions the attention matrix into blocks of size `block_len` (default: 128) and determines at the block level which blocks contain at least one valid attention pair. This block-level sparsity is what makes flex attention efficient — entire blocks of the attention matrix can be skipped rather than individually masking positions.

The block mask construction also respects auxiliary tokens (e.g., species or assay embeddings prepended to the gene sequence). The padding mask is extended to cover auxiliary token positions, and the concatenation of auxiliary and gene embeddings means the causal mask operates over the full sequence including aux prefixes.

Sources: [masks.py](src/transcriptformer/model/masks.py#L1-L17), [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L243-L268)

## Data Flow Through the Encoder

The complete data flow from raw batch data through the encoder follows a precise sequence. First, gene token indices are right-shifted (prepending a `[START]` token) and log-counts are computed as `log1p(count + eps)`. Gene tokens are embedded via `PretrainedEmbeddings`, and auxiliary tokens are embedded separately and concatenated to the front of the sequence. The block mask is compiled from the composed causal + padding mask. The score modification closure captures the log-counts tensor. The encoder then processes the embedded sequence through all layers, producing contextualized representations for both the auxiliary prefix and the gene positions. After the encoder, auxiliary outputs are sliced off, leaving only gene-level representations for downstream heads.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as BatchData
    participant M as Transcriptformer
    participant E as TranscriptEncoder
    participant L as "FlexAttnTransformerLayer xN"

    B->>M: gene_tokens, counts, aux_tokens
    M->>M: Right-shift tokens, compute log_counts
    M->>M: Embed gene tokens + aux tokens, concatenate
    M->>M: Compile block_mask = create_block_mask(pad ∧ causal)
    M->>M: Build score_mod = _score_mod_factory(log_counts)
    M->>E: forward(x, score_mod, block_mask)
    loop For each layer
        E->>L: layer(x, score_mod, block_mask)
        L->>L: "PreNorm → FlexAttn(+score_mod, block_mask) → Residual"
        L->>L: "PreNorm → FFN → Residual"
        L-->>E: x (updated)
    end
    E-->>M: transformer_output
    M->>M: "Slice off aux prefix → gene_output"
    M->>M: "Route to CountDecoderHead / mean_embeddings"
```

Sources: [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L232-L310), [layers.py](src/transcriptformer/model/layers.py#L245-L252)

## Configuration Parameters

All encoder-related hyperparameters are defined in the `ModelConfig` dataclass. The following table summarizes the parameters that directly control the flex attention encoder's behavior:

| Parameter | Type | Default | Affects | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `embed_dim` | `int` | `2048` | Encoder, Embeddings | Model / embedding dimension |
| `num_heads` | `int` | `16` | Encoder | Number of attention heads per layer |
| `num_layers` | `int` | `12` | Encoder | Number of transformer layers |
| `model_dim` | `int` | `2048` | Encoder | Feed-forward hidden dimension |
| `dropout` | `float` | `0.1` | Encoder, Embeddings | Dropout rate |
| `activation` | `str` | `"gelu"` | Encoder | Activation: `relu`, `gelu`, or `silu` |
| `attn_bias` | `bool` | `False` | Encoder | Bias in attention Q/K/V/output projections |
| `fw_bias` | `bool` | `False` | Encoder | Bias in feed-forward linear layers |
| `softcap` | `int` | `10` | Score Mod | Softcap value for attention logit bounding |
| `block_len` | `int` | `128` | Block Mask | Block size for flex attention sparse masking |
| `seq_len` | `int` | `2047` | Block Mask | Maximum gene sequence length |
| `aux_len` | `int` | `1` | Block Mask | Number of auxiliary tokens prepended |
| `compile_block_mask` | `bool` | `True` | Encoder, Block Mask | Compile block mask creation + flex attention |
| `log_counts_eps` | `float` | `1e-6` | Score Mod | Epsilon for numerical stability in log-counts |

A validation constraint enforces that `(seq_len + aux_len) % block_len == 0`, ensuring the block mask can partition the full sequence (genes + aux tokens) into complete blocks without remainder.

Sources: [dataclasses.py](src/transcriptformer/data/dataclasses.py#L16-L76)

## Design Rationale and Trade-offs

**Why Flex Attention over Standard Attention?** Standard PyTorch attention (`F.scaled_dot_product_attention`) supports a fixed set of attention masks (causal, padding) but provides no hook for injecting custom score modifications. Flex attention's `score_mod` callback is essential for the count-informed bias, which is a first-class architectural feature of TranscriptFormer — expression magnitude must influence attention, not just gene identity. The block-sparse masking also provides computational savings over dense attention on variable-length gene sequences where many positions are padding.

**Why Pre-Norm over Post-Norm?** Pre-norm stabilizes gradient flow through deep stacks (the model uses 12 layers by default). In post-norm architectures, the residual path is modulated by LayerNorm, which can cause gradient vanishing in deep models. Pre-norm keeps the residual path clean, allowing gradients to flow unimpeded through the skip connections.

**Why Compile Flex Attention?** The `torch.compile(fullgraph=True)` wrapper on `flex_attention` fuses the attention score computation, score modification, and softmax into a single GPU kernel. Without compilation, each operation launches a separate kernel, and the element-wise score modification becomes a bottleneck. The `compile_block_mask` flag additionally controls whether `create_block_mask` is compiled, which accelerates mask construction for repeated batches of the same shape.

**Softcapping as a Regularizer**: The `softcap` parameter (default: 10) bounds attention scores via `softcap * tanh(score / softcap)`, which maps the real line to `(-softcap, +softcap)`. This prevents any single attention head from producing extremely large logits — particularly important given that the count-informed bias can be large for highly expressed genes. The same softcapping mechanism is also applied in the gene ID prediction head (see [Count Decoder and Expression Prediction](7-count-decoder-and-expression-prediction)), creating a consistent regularization strategy across the model.

Sources: [layers.py](src/transcriptformer/model/layers.py#L27-L98), [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L218-L268), [losses.py](src/transcriptformer/model/losses.py#L24-L38)

## What Comes Next

The encoder's output feeds into two downstream paths: the **count decoder head** for expression prediction and the **mean embedding function** for cell-level representations. The count-informed attention bias and softcapping mechanisms described here directly shape the loss landscape covered in [Zero-Truncated Poisson Loss](8-zero-truncated-poisson-loss). The causal masking strategy connects to the broader autoregressive training design discussed in [Architecture Overview](4-architecture-overview). For the embedding extraction path — where `emb_mode=True` removes the causal constraint — see [Cell and Contextual Gene Embeddings](14-cell-and-contextual-gene-embeddings).

# Count Decoder and Expression Prediction



The Count Decoder is the prediction head that transforms TranscriptFormer's transformer encoder output into per-gene expression rate estimates. It is the architectural bridge between the contextual gene representations produced by the [Flex Attention Transformer Encoder](6-flex-attention-transformer-encoder) and the actual count values that define a cell's transcriptomic profile. Unlike generative language models that decode into a discrete token vocabulary, TranscriptFormer's decoder produces a **continuous rate parameter** μ for each gene position—this rate is then consumed by the [Zero-Truncated Poisson Loss](8-zero-truncated-poisson-loss) to compute training likelihoods. Understanding this component is essential for anyone modifying the model's prediction behavior, adapting it to new data regimes, or interpreting the meaning of the `mu` output key.

Sources: [model.py](src/transcriptformer/model/model.py#L1-L27), [layers.py](src/transcriptformer/model/layers.py#L229-L329)

## From Encoder Output to Expression Rate: The Data Flow

The count decoder does not operate on the transformer output alone. A critical architectural detail is that the decoder receives a **concatenation of two signals**: the transformer's contextual output (which has attended to all prior genes via causal attention) and the original input gene embedding (which carries the pretrained protein identity signal). This skip-connection-style concatenation doubles the input dimensionality and ensures that the decoder always has direct access to the identity of the gene whose count it is predicting, without relying solely on the encoder's ability to preserve that information through multiple attention layers.

The following diagram traces the complete path from raw batch data through the decoder to the final μ prediction:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["BatchData\ngene_token_indices, gene_counts"] --> B["Right-shift gene tokens\nprepend [START], drop last"]
    A --> C["Gene Embeddings\nPretrainedEmbeddings(right_shifted)"]
    A --> D["Gene Embeddings\nPretrainedEmbeddings(original)"]

    B --> E["Transformer Encoder\nTranscriptEncoder"]
    C --> E
    E --> F["gene_output\n(batch, seq_len, embed_dim)"]

    F --> G["Concatenation\n[encoder_output ∥ input_embeddings]"]
    D --> G
    G --> H["conditioned_output\n(batch, seq_len, 2*embed_dim)"]

    H --> I["CountDecoderHead (μ)"]
    A --> J["Padding Mask\n_pad_mask(gene_tokens)"]
    J --> I

    I --> K{"Link Function\nmu_link_fn?"}
    K -->|softmax| L["MaskedSoftmax → proportions\n× total_counts = μ"]
    K -->|sigmoid| M["Sigmoid-bounded rates"]
    K -->|softplus| N["Softplus-positive rates"]
```
